title: The Trigger Isn't a Revenue Number. It's a Question You Can No Longer Answer Alone.
excerpt: Owners often wait for a revenue milestone before bringing in extra financial support. The real signal shows up earlier, in the questions they can no longer answer with confidence on their own.
content:
Plenty of owner-led businesses carry a number in their head. Once revenue hits five million, or ten, that's when a fractional CFO gets a seat at the table. It's a tidy plan, and it's almost always measuring the wrong thing, because revenue was never the real signal they were waiting for.

Two businesses turning over six million dollars a year can sit in completely different places. One sells a single product to a handful of long-standing customers through one bank facility. The other runs three revenue lines out of a leased warehouse, carries a working capital facility with covenants attached, and has a silent partner asking sharper questions every quarter. Same number on the top line. A very different amount of financial judgement required to run it well.

The pattern we see across owner-led businesses is that the real trigger isn't a milestone on the P&L. It's a moment when the owner realises they are the only person in the business who can answer a particular financial question, and that answering it alone is starting to cost more than it should, in time, in sleep, or in a decision made later than it needed to be.

Revenue Is a Lagging, Unreliable Trigger

Revenue tells you how much is moving through the business. It says almost nothing about how much judgement that movement requires. A professional services firm billing four partners' time looks financially simple right up until it adds a second office, a different fee structure for one service line, and a bank facility to fund the fit-out. A trades business can carry the same turnover for three straight years while quietly adding a second finance facility, a bigger vehicle fleet and a handful of fixed-price contracts that behave nothing like the time and materials work the owner built the business on. The revenue line barely moved. The amount of judgement required behind it moved a great deal.

Waiting for a round number to arrive means the business is already running on borrowed judgement by the time anyone notices, because the complexity usually shows up well before the growth does.

The Signals Worth Watching Instead

Three signals tend to matter more than any figure on the income statement, and each one is easy to spot once an owner starts looking for it rather than waiting for it to become unavoidable.

  • Every meaningful financial call in the business runs through one person, with nobody in the room to pressure test it before the decision gets made.
  • Complexity has quietly outgrown the reporting. A new finance facility, a second location, an additional revenue line or an entity structure that didn't exist two years ago, sitting on top of the same monthly report that worked fine when the business was simpler.
  • Someone outside the business, a bank, an investor or a prospective buyer, asks a question that takes days to answer rather than minutes, which usually means the business has outgrown its own visibility into itself.

None of these signals require a crisis to show up. They tend to arrive quietly, one at a time, which is exactly why a revenue milestone feels like the easier thing to wait for. It's visible. These three usually aren't, until the cost of ignoring them is.

What Changes Once the Signal Shows Up

Bringing in a fractional CFO partnership at this point isn't about replacing the owner's judgement. It's about giving that judgement a second, experienced perspective before a decision gets made rather than after. The work usually looks less like a bigger reporting pack and more like someone sitting across the table who has seen the specific pattern before, whether that's a facility renewal, a pricing decision sitting on sentiment rather than margin, or a question from a buyer the business hasn't had to answer under this much scrutiny before.

The engagement doesn't need to start at full scale either. Partnership tiers exist precisely because the right level of involvement in year one of noticing the signal is rarely the same as the right level three years later, once the business has grown into the complexity it was starting to carry. For a business that's still deciding whether the signal is real, what a fractional CFO actually does day to day is worth reading before worrying about which tier fits.

None of this changes what a bookkeeper or compliance accountant does. They keep the ledger accurate and the lodgements on time, which matters just as much once the business gets more complex, not less. A fractional CFO sits on top of that work, turning accurate numbers into a decision the owner no longer has to make entirely on their own.

Most owners already know, somewhere, when they've started answering these questions alone more often than feels comfortable. The useful next step usually isn't guessing at a revenue number that hasn't arrived yet. It's naming the question that's been sitting unanswered a little too long, and bringing it to a discovery call before it has to be answered under pressure.

faqs.q: How do I know if my business is ready for a fractional CFO in Australia?
faqs.a: Readiness usually shows up as a pattern rather than a single event. If financial decisions increasingly run through one person with nobody to pressure test them, if the business has added complexity like a new facility or revenue line faster than its reporting has kept up, or if outside parties are asking questions that take days to answer, those are stronger signals than any specific revenue figure.

faqs.q: At what revenue size does an SME typically need a fractional CFO?
faqs.a: There's no reliable revenue threshold, because complexity and turnover don't move at the same pace. A business on three million dollars with multiple finance facilities and revenue lines can need more financial judgement than one on eight million running a single simple model. The fractional CFO partnership is built in tiers so the level of involvement can match the actual complexity, not a round number.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a fractional CFO and a bookkeeper?
faqs.a: A bookkeeper keeps the ledger current, reconciles accounts and handles the day to day transactional record. A fractional CFO sits above that work, turning accurate figures into decisions about pricing, cash, facilities and growth. Neither role replaces the other, and most owner-led businesses need both working alongside each other rather than one instead of the other.

faqs.q: Can a small business afford a fractional CFO before it feels ready?
faqs.a: Most engagements are designed to flex rather than demand a large fixed commitment from day one. The fractional CFO cost guide sets out how pricing tracks the level of involvement, which means a business can start at a lighter tier and step up once the complexity genuinely warrants it, rather than waiting until the cost of going without feels larger than the fee itself.

faqs.q: What questions should an SME owner be able to answer about their own numbers?
faqs.a: At a minimum, an owner should be able to say with confidence what's driving margin up or down this quarter, how much cash is tied up in debtors and stock, and what a lender or buyer would ask first if they looked at the business tomorrow. Struggling to answer any of these quickly is usually a stronger signal than a revenue figure.

faqs.q: Does bringing in a fractional CFO mean the owner loses control of decisions?
faqs.a: No. The role is to bring an experienced second perspective to the table, not to take decisions away from the owner. Most owner-led businesses find the opposite happens, decisions get made with more confidence because there's someone across the table who has seen the specific pattern before and can pressure test the thinking.

faqs.q: How do I start a conversation about whether a fractional CFO is right for my business?
faqs.a: The simplest starting point is naming the specific question that's been sitting unanswered, rather than asking in the abstract whether the business is ready. A discovery call is usually enough to work out whether the signal is real and what level of support actually fits, without committing to anything before that conversation happens.
